learning_h2_html: You're the hacker. You're also the target.
learning_intro_p_html: Every player is attacking and defending at the same time. Racing to steal a Data Flag while building the defenses to stop everyone else from stealing yours. One turn. Two jobs. No excuses.
learning_section_label: What you'll actually understand after playing

concept_cards.title: Attacker Mindset
concept_cards.body_html: Attackers don't strike randomly. They follow a sequence. The Cyber Kill Chain maps every stage from the first bit of reconnaissance to the final objective. Playing the attack side teaches you how adversaries think, plan, and move, and why disrupting any single stage can collapse the entire operation.

concept_cards.icon_svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#62b517" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 2L4 6v6c0 5.5 3.5 10.7 8 12 4.5-1.3 8-6.5 8-12V6L12 2z"/><path d="M9 12l2 2 4-4" stroke="#d1db24" stroke-width="2"/></svg>
concept_cards.title: Defender Mindset
concept_cards.body_html: Defense isn't one big wall. It's a complete posture. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework gives defenders a structured approach: Identify what you're protecting, Protect it, Detect threats early, Respond fast, and Recover fully. With Govern at the center, providing the policies, roles, and decisions that hold it all together. Every gap in that posture is a stage of the Kill Chain a defender failed to cover.

concept_cards.icon_svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="#62b517" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M1 4v6h6"/><path d="M23 20v-6h-6"/><path d="M20.49 9A9 9 0 0 0 5.64 5.64L1 10"/><path d="M23 14l-4.64 4.36A9 9 0 0 1 3.51 15" stroke="#d1db24"/></svg>
concept_cards.title: The Cycle of Cyberwarfare
concept_cards.body_html: Attack and defense are never finished. They feed each other. Defenders add controls to disrupt the Kill Chain; attackers find ways around them; defenders adapt again. That perpetual loop is the Cycle of Cyberwarfare. And once you see it, you can use it as a mental model to make sense of any threat, breach, or security decision you'll ever encounter.

concept_cards.title: You are CyberFluent
concept_cards.body_html: Understanding that cycle means you can break down any cybersecurity incident or topic and ask the right questions. It won't make you a cyber expert. But it means you can appropriately challenge one. Instead of waiting for the latest checklist from experts to tell you what to think, you'll have the mental model to think critically yourself. Rather than just accepting what you're told or begrudgingly going along with it, you'll understand enough to be genuinely on the same page and push toward the best solution.

workshop_h2_html: The interactive demo supports the physical game — run only what you need.
workshop_intro_p_html: The Play Now demo includes a built-in interactive tutorial with three independent sections you can toggle on or off. It works alongside the physical game: use it to explain rules, walk through concepts projected on screen, or let participants follow along at their own pace.

workshop_cards.title: Suggested Workshop Flow
workshop_cards.body_html:
Before the session: Ask participants to open the demo and run the Context section on their own. This covers the Cyber Kill Chain, the NIST Framework, and the Cycle of Cyberwarfare — so you arrive with shared vocabulary, not a lecture.

At the start of the session (in person): Walk through the Physical Game Setup and How to Play sections together — projected or on individual screens — so everyone sets up and learns the rules at the same pace.

Online session: Skip the setup section entirely. The demo handles the rules walkthrough interactively as participants play.

workshop_cards.title: Run only the sections you need
workshop_cards.body_html: The tutorial lets you toggle three sections independently: Context for Learning Objectives, Physical Game Setup, and How to Play Instructions. If participants already know the concepts, skip Context. If you're playing online, skip Setup. Mix and match to fit your session without sitting through parts that don't apply.
